subject: Cluster vs individuals and transect length issues

messages.author: feb147fd0dff04d3
messages.subject: Cluster vs individuals and transect length issues
parts:
Dear Distance-samplers
I am entering data from a line-transect distance sampling survey on long-tailed macaques.
I have tried different approaches according to different literature and I get very different results.

My questions:

1. Should I choose inidviduals or cluster, when I have perpendicular distance to sub-group centre (PD to centre of measurable individuals)? It is not possible to measure PD to group centre or to estimate group spread of the large groups of macaques in very dense vegetation.

2. We walked transects of approx 4.5km at approx 1km/hour one way in the morning, rested for 2 hours, and then walked back. Covering the 4.5km two times in one day. We did not record sub-groups we had seen before, or sub-groups of same sizes and composition at same positions to reduce double-counting. Should I then record a transect length of 4.5km or 9km?

I thank you in advance for any advice you have to offer.
Malene

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Cluster vs individuals and transect length issues
parts:
Malene

Have a look at this paper


Visit http://distancesampling.org/dbib.html and search for it to give you a direct link.  This paper suggests recording the centre distance separately for each individual in the group (i.e. a group of 4 with a centre PD of 11m, would have 4 records of single individuals all located at 11m).

Your second question is more complicated.  It would seem that 9km would guard against some double counting.  Are these transects cut through vegetation?  It would make the analysis (and inference) more reliable if the return leg did not retrace the outbound leg.

messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Cluster vs individuals and transect length issues
parts:
Just adding to Eric’s comments, it would definitely be wrong to count the effort twice, because you didn’t count the animals twice.  So 4.5km, and use only the data on the outward leg.  If you try using the return data, movement will cause upward bias in density estimates, but recording effort as 9km would only work if you recorded all detected animals on the return trip, not just those previously not detected.  And yes, in these circumstances, analyse individuals, not groups.

 

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Cluster vs individuals and transect length issues
parts:
Dear Eric and Stephen
I have tried to run my data as individuals several times, and I keep getting the warning message:
Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity 
for 4 of the 5 models (2-5). 

Distance then chooses the 5th model which has the warning message, but the lowest AIC (2300).
I believe that the warning message stems form my data being obtained in very diverse habitats and therefore not meeting the assumption of detection decreasing with distance.

If I manually choose the model with no warning message, model no 1 - half normal key cosine with 0 adjustments and monoticity constraints, the tests runs perfectly without any warning messages.
However, this model has the highest AIC (2500).

For model 5 I have a density of 30 and an abundance of 7500
For model 1 I have a density of 18 and an abundance of 4700
As you can see the difference is quite large.

Which model should I choose?
I hope you can help.
Thank you for your time.
Malene

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Cluster vs individuals and transect length issues
parts:
Malene

The issue causing the warning is adjustment terms.  Warnings are issued by Distance with the programme has two instructions it is trying to perform, but those instructions are in conflict.  In this case the instructions are to a) achieve the best fit to the data and b) not have a fitted detection function that increases as a function of distance.  Warnings do not necessarily indicate problems as much as suggestions to look deeper into the fitting process.

These add flexibility to the key function models, and permit the fitted detection function to have wiggles in it.  Sometimes those wiggles cause the detection to rise, rather than fall, over some distance range.  When the detection function rises, this violates the principle of monotonicity--that a detection function should only decrease as a function of distance.

When analysing your data from animal groups as individuals, this will invariably cause some "lumps" in your data that the models with adjustments may be trying to fit.  Besides the AIC score, you ought also to be examining the goodness of fit statistic.  You might expect some poorer fit caused by the lumps in your sightings, but assess the absolute fit of your models (via goodness of fit tests) in addition to assessing relative fit (via AIC).

** Warning: One or more cluster sizes are coded as -1. Distance assumes -1 to mean a cluster of undetermined size. These observations are used for estimating detection probability and encounter rate, but not cluster size. **

      ** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. **
** Warning: Size bias adjustment has increased expected cluster size. **
I have read that entering the subgroups as clusters is also acceptable, however, if asked I still wouldnt be able to estimate group spread.
Is this acceptable? The estimate is fairly close to the estimate when entering them as individuals, wheer Distance chooses the test with lowest AIC:

Would you choose to enter my data as subgroups as clusters?
Thank you again for your time.
Malene

onsdag den 20. juni 2018 kl. 14.46.34 UTC+2 skrev Eric Rexstad:

Malene

The issue causing the warning is adjustment terms.  Warnings are issued by Distance with the programme has two instructions it is trying to perform, but those instructions are in conflict.  In this case the instructions are to a) achieve the best fit to the data and b) not have a fitted detection function that increases as a function of distance.  Warnings do not necessarily indicate problems as much as suggestions to look deeper into the fitting process.

These add flexibility to the key function models, and permit the fitted detection function to have wiggles in it.  Sometimes those wiggles cause the detection to rise, rather than fall, over some distance range.  When the detection function rises, this violates the principle of monotonicity--that a detection function should only decrease as a function of distance.

When analysing your data from animal groups as individuals, this will invariably cause some "lumps" in your data that the models with adjustments may be trying to fit.  Besides the AIC score, you ought also to be examining the goodness of fit statistic.  You might expect some poorer fit caused by the lumps in your sightings, but assess the absolute fit of your models (via goodness of fit tests) in addition to assessing relative fit (via AIC).

parts:
Malene

Comparison of AIC across datasets (individuals vs clusters) is uninformative and will not serve as a guide to the best way to proceed.

I think you find yourself in a position of compromise; analysing data as groups has less over-dispersion in the histogram of distances and hence a better fit.  However you are uncomfortable with the measure of group size and location of group centre.

To circumvent the issues of group size measurement, data can be analysed as individuals.  This brings in the over-dispersion and subsequent deterioration in model fit metrics.  I'm afraid this is as far as objectivity in analysis can take you.  From this point you must reconcile which of the compromises you prefer.
